As vibe coding — that is, writing programs using artificial intelligence prompts — becomes increasingly popular, the number of new applications submitted to the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026, yet downloads have grown by only 2%. The following is the full report.

The number of new app submissions has skyrocketed, while downloads lag far behind

The New York Times published a report today, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, indicating that although the number of new applications submitted to the App Store in the first half of 2026 doubled, downloads only rose by 2%.

The report also mentioned two developers who have been consistently releasing vibe coding applications on the App Store: Marco Pérez plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to devote himself full-time to app development, while David Svensson has launched 11 niche applications over the past five months, treating vibe coding as a hobby rather than a career.

Excerpts from the report are as follows:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never developed a mobile application before. He spent five weeks during the winter researching "vibe coding" AI tools to create prototypes, then spent another two weeks preparing for App Store submission. His app InfoDrizzle has performed reasonably well, accumulating 1,300 downloads to date and earning approximately US$500 in profit. Pérez's next application has been even more popular. He spent about a week in May launching Stappa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps, which has recorded 20,000 downloads to date and earned approximately US$3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian told The New York Times that the surge in submissions has created another problem: as previously reported, the App Store's review process is under enormous pressure.

Ajemian pointed out that "Apple has always been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple "welcomes a new generation of developers using the latest tools to build and launch applications at an unprecedented pace."

He also emphasised that all applications "regardless of whether they were developed through vibe coding, must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have always trusted."
